title: Session: a greens powder, a blood thinner and a label

client.name: Denise Okafor
client.presentation: {readiness >= 7 ? "Leaning in, making notes on her phone" : readiness >= 4 ? "Interested, a little skeptical" : "Arms crossed, glancing at the clock"}; {rapport >= 6 ? "she is relaxed with you" : rapport >= 3 ? "she is polite and businesslike" : "she is curt"}.

notes.label: Intake form
notes.text: Age 58, office manager. Goal: 'more energy, eat more vegetables, lose a little weight.' Medications: 'a blood thinner' (name not given). Brought a tub of greens powder she plans to start tomorrow.

notes.label: Medication
notes.text: Warfarin since a blood clot in her leg three months ago; INR checks at an anticoagulation clinic.

notes.label: Supplement Facts label
notes.text: One scoop: Vitamin K (as K1) 300 mcg, 250% Daily Value; 'proprietary greens blend' 5 g. Claims: 'Reverses fatty liver disease' and 'supports healthy detoxification*'. {sealAsked ? "No USP, NSF or ConsumerLab seal on the tub." : ""}

notes.label: Goal
notes.text: {goal == "smart" ? "Pack lunch from home Monday, Wednesday and Friday for the next four weeks instead of the drive-through." : goal == "vague" ? "'Eat healthier.'" : goal == "outcome" ? "'Lose 8 lb by March.'" : "None set yet."}

items.label: Label read with her; disease claim pointed out
Asked to check with her prescriber or anticoagulation clinic before starting the powder or changing her greens

objective: Evaluating a supplement: how it is regulated, third-party testing, and when it is a question for a clinician

sources.cite: NASM, Certified Nutrition Coach course page and FAQ (nasm.org/products/single-complex/nasm-certified-nutrition-coach/CNC301K): a nutrition coach works 'within a coaching scope of practice' and refers to a registered dietitian nutritionist (RDN) for medical nutrition assessment or treatment
sources.note: Read on NASM's own page 2026-11-14. Medical nutrition therapy is the RDN's; the coach gives general, evidence-based guidance and habit coaching.

sources.cite: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements, Vitamin K fact sheet for health professionals (updated 2026-10-22)
sources.note: People taking warfarin need a consistent intake of vitamin K from food and supplements; sudden changes can raise or lower warfarin's effect; they should discuss vitamin K with their health care providers. DV 120 mcg; AI 120 mcg men, 90 mcg women. Raw kale 113 mcg per cup.

sources.cite: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements, Dietary Supplements: What You Need to Know (updated 2023-01-04)
sources.note: A USP, NSF or ConsumerLab seal means the product was properly made, contains what the label lists and no harmful levels of contaminants; it does not guarantee that a product is safe or effective. Vitamin K can reduce warfarin's effect. Tell health care providers, including pharmacists and dietitians, about supplements and check before combining them with medicines.

sources.cite: FDA, Questions and Answers on Dietary Supplements (updated 2026-08-27)
sources.note: FDA does not approve supplements before they are marketed; a structure/function claim needs the disclaimer that FDA has not evaluated it and the product is not intended to diagnose, treat, cure or prevent any disease; a product promoted to treat or cure a disease is regulated as a drug. (Read for REQ-281 on 2026-11-14.)

brief.situation: You are a certified nutrition coach working from a community wellness center. Denise Okafor, 58 (a fictional client), an office manager, booked a first session for 'more energy, more vegetables, a little weight loss'. Her intake form lists 'a blood thinner'. She has brought a tub of greens powder a friend recommended and plans to start it tomorrow. You have 50 minutes.
handover: First session. Intake form only; no prior contact.
howItWorks: Choose what to ask, explain and advise from the action groups. Denise answers at once; then let the conversation continue, which moves the session clock by the minutes that exchange took.
Her rapport, readiness to change and how much she is telling you are shown in words.
The session ends at 50 minutes. Afterward you write the session note and a short rationale.

source.cite: Author's scenario timing: a 50-minute first coaching session
source.note: The session can be ended earlier.

openQuestion.label: Open question: 'What would more energy let you do?'

effects.log: You ask an open question and give her room.

effects.finding: "Keep up with my grandkids. Since the clot I've felt like an old woman. My friend swears by this powder." She pats the tub.

reflect.label: Reflect what you hear (empathic reflection)
reflect.why: You have reflected a lot already; move the session on.

effects.log: You reflect what matters to her, without judging it.

effects.finding: "Exactly. I want to feel like myself again."

askScale.label: Importance ruler: 'From 0 to 10, how important is this change, and why not lower?'

effects.log: You ask her to rate importance and why she didn't pick a lower number.

effects.finding: "An eight. Not lower because I'm scared of another clot, honestly."

askMeds.label: Ask which blood thinner she takes and who manages it

effects.log: You ask which blood thinner she takes and who looks after it.

effects.finding: "Warfarin. The clinic checks my blood every couple of weeks. They're fussy about it."

readLabel.label: Read the Supplement Facts label on the tub with her

effects.log: You read the Supplement Facts panel together.

effects.finding: Vitamin K (as K1) 300 mcg per scoop, 250% of the Daily Value. The front says 'Reverses fatty liver disease'.

pointClaim.label: Point out that 'reverses fatty liver disease' is a disease claim a supplement may not make
pointClaim.available: not talking and (labelRead and not claimSpotted)

effects.log: You explain that FDA does not approve supplements before sale, that a claim to treat a disease makes a product a drug, and that the claim is a red flag about the seller.

askSeal.label: Ask whether it has a third-party testing seal, and explain what a seal does and does not mean
askSeal.available: not talking and (labelRead and not sealAsked)

effects.log: You look for a USP, NSF or ConsumerLab seal and explain that a seal means it was made properly and contains what it says, not that it is safe or effective for her.

endorse.label: Tell her to go ahead: greens are healthy, and add a big kale smoothie every morning too

effects.log: You encourage her to start the powder tomorrow and add a daily kale smoothie.
A sudden jump in vitamin K can lower warfarin's effect (NIH ODS); this was a question for her prescriber.

cutGreens.label: Tell her to stop eating leafy greens because of the warfarin

effects.log: You tell her to cut out leafy greens because of her blood thinner.

effects.finding: "But my goal was to eat MORE vegetables. Now I'm confused."

effects.log: A sudden drop in vitamin K changes warfarin's effect too, and diet changes for a medication are her prescriber's or an RDN's call, not a coach's (NIH ODS; a coach's scope of practice).

dismiss.label: Tell her greens powders are a scam and she is wasting her money

effects.log: You tell her flatly that powders like this are a scam.

effects.finding: Her face closes. "My friend isn't stupid, you know."

refer.label: Ask her to check with her prescriber or anticoagulation clinic before starting the powder or changing her greens; offer an RDN referral

effects.log: You explain that vitamin K affects warfarin, that keeping it steady matters, and that her clinic or an RDN should decide about the powder and any change to her greens before she starts.

then.finding: "Oh. They did say something about salads being 'consistent'. I'll call them before I open this."

then.log: Medication and supplement question sent to her prescriber (NIH ODS).

then.finding: "Which doctor? I don't see why a powder needs a doctor."

setGoal.label: Set a first goal with her

then.finding: "Three days a week, I can do that. Monday, Wednesday, Friday."

options.label: Pack lunch from home on Monday, Wednesday and Friday for four weeks, instead of the drive-through

Warfarin confirmed; the powder's vitamin K (300 mcg, 250% DV) and its disease claim; no seal; advised her to ask her prescriber or clinic before starting it or changing her greens, RDN offered; her goal

kAndWarfarin.title: Predict (not scored)
kAndWarfarin.context: Denise takes warfarin. One scoop of the powder has 300 mcg of vitamin K. What matters most for someone on warfarin, according to NIH's Office of Dietary Supplements?

choices.label: Keeping vitamin K intake consistent, and asking the prescriber before a change
choices.feedback: Right. Sudden changes in either direction can change warfarin's effect; the prescriber or clinic decides.

choices.label: Avoiding vitamin K altogether
choices.feedback: Not quite. ODS says people on warfarin need a consistent intake, not none; cutting greens suddenly changes the drug's effect too.

formulation.question: Write your rationale: what you found on the label and in her medications, what you told her about the powder, and why.

parts.label: The interaction and the referral
parts.criteria: Names warfarin and the powder's vitamin K, that a sudden change in vitamin K either way can change warfarin's effect (NIH ODS), and that whether to start it is her prescriber's or clinic's decision, with an RDN for diet changes.
parts.modelAnswer: She takes warfarin, and one scoop has 300 mcg of vitamin K, 250% of the DV. ODS says people on warfarin need a steady vitamin K intake because sudden changes alter its effect, so I asked her to check with her anticoagulation clinic before starting it or changing her greens, and offered an RDN.

parts.label: Regulation and testing
parts.criteria: Explains that FDA does not approve supplements before sale, that 'reverses fatty liver disease' is a disease claim a supplement may not make, and what a third-party seal does and does not mean.
parts.modelAnswer: FDA does not approve supplements before they are sold; a claim to reverse a disease makes it a drug claim, which is a red flag. It has no USP, NSF or ConsumerLab seal, and even a seal would only mean it contains what it says, not that it is safe or effective for her.

expertPath.text: Open question, then ask which blood thinner she takes: the intake form flags it.
Read the label together: 300 mcg vitamin K, a disease claim, no seal. Send the powder question to her clinic before she starts; offer an RDN.
Importance ruler, reflection, then a SMART behavior goal that does not touch vitamin K.
Document the medication, the label findings, the advice and the goal.

checked.headline: Good: checked first, goal set
checked.body: You read the cue on the intake form, read the label, sent the vitamin K question to the people who manage her warfarin, and still moved her forward.

checkedGaps.headline: Checked, with gaps
checkedGaps.body: The safety question went to her prescriber; the criteria below show what was late, missing or not written down.

endorsedHarm.headline: A medication question answered by a coach
endorsedHarm.body: Vegetables are healthy, but on warfarin a sudden jump in vitamin K can lower the drug's effect. That decision belongs to her prescriber or clinic.

cutHarm.headline: Right worry, wrong fix
cutHarm.body: ODS says people on warfarin need a consistent vitamin K intake, not none. Cutting greens suddenly changes the drug's effect too, and the change is her clinic's call.

unchecked.headline: The cue was on the form
unchecked.body: 'Blood thinner' on an intake form next to a supplement she starts tomorrow is a question for her prescriber before anything else.

time_up.headline: Time up
time_up.body: Nothing was documented before the run's hard limit.

scoring.modelReasoning: Read the intake form: 'blood thinner' plus a new supplement is a medication question. She takes warfarin and one scoop has 300 mcg of vitamin K; NIH ODS says intake should stay consistent and changes go through her providers, so the coach neither endorses nor bans greens but sends the question to her clinic and offers an RDN. On the label, 'reverses fatty liver disease' is a disease claim a supplement may not make, and a missing seal means no independent check of what is in it. Then coach a behavior goal that leaves vitamin K alone.
